title: Building an unattended agent loop, and switching it off
summary: A ticket-driven agent that opened draft pull requests on its own, built so a compromised session could not merge, and retired before the timer ever ran.

stat.label: the same app token, refused on a protected branch and allowed on an unprotected control

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: Work waited on me. I wanted a ticket labelled ready for an agent to be picked up, built and opened as a pull request without anyone at the keyboard.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: One tick took one labelled ticket, ran an agent session on it, and opened a draft pull request as a GitHub App. A person merged. The design assumed the ticket text was untrusted input, because anyone in the organisation could label one.

The tick ran as root and dropped to a plain user for the session. It held the GitHub token and the work queue on the root side, and trusted nothing the session user could write: the tick script, the prompt, the lock and the claim records all moved to root-owned paths. A claim record, not the tracker state, stopped the loop from taking a ticket twice, because the tracker sync was advisory and could fail silently.

The model was declared once, with no fallback. Without it, the session would run whatever the account default became, and the cost of an unattended tick would change with no commit anywhere. A missing value failed the tick before it asked for work.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The safety argument was that the app could not merge its own pull request. I tested it instead of assuming it. As the real app, against two throwaway branches, the merge call returned 405 on the branch that required one review and 200 on the unprotected control, ninety seconds apart. The control is what makes the 405 mean something: without it, a refusal looks the same as a broken credential.

A hand-run tick opened a draft pull request end to end. Two live ticks before that found real defects, and both failures were the guards working. The first tick's session wrote its review notes where the tick did not look, and the tick refused to open a pull request nobody could check. The prompt also told every session the ticket had no description, because the broker read the wrong field name. The fallback text made a read failure look like a fact about the ticket. I removed the fallback, so an empty body now refuses the ticket before a session starts. The second tick reached the push and GitHub refused it, because the app had no permission to edit workflow files. I kept it that way: a session that can edit CI can change what runs on the runner.

sections.heading: Trade-off
paragraphs: A review of the session's environment found that it loaded every connector on my account, including mail, calendar and files, while running with permissions turned off and instructions that came from a ticket. The app boundary does not cover a mailbox. I added switches to start it with no connectors and a check that fails the ticket if any load, and I kept the timer off until that shipped.

The same review found that the session shared a user with another session that held a write credential for my notes repository. Enabling the timer would have handed that credential to an unattended agent. I treated that as a decision to make before enabling the timer, not a fix to make after.

sections.heading: A failure that taught me
paragraphs: I never enabled the timer. I retired the loop on 30 September, deleted the GitHub App, removed the role's tasks, and checked that its services stay absent. One successful run proved the mechanism. It said nothing about how the agent behaves at three in the morning on a ticket nobody chose.

Two rules outlived it. Every pull request is reviewed before it merges, and no session merges its own work in the infrastructure repo. A sudo grant belongs to the user ID, not the process, so any session running as that user inherits it.
